summary: This note describes the British decimal five pence (5p) coin, a unit equal to five one-hundredths of a pound sterling. Its obverse has shown Queen Elizabeth II since its introduction on 23 April 1968, replacing the shilling ahead of decimalisation in 1971. The note covers the smaller version introduced in 1990, the four Queen portraits used (latest by Jody Clark in 2015), and the current reverse showing a segment of the Royal Shield from 2008. The text is duplicated in the source.
one_line: Overview of the British decimal five pence (5p) coin, its Queen Elizabeth II portraits, and its reverse designs.
key_facts: The British decimal five pence (5p) coin is a unit of currency equaling five one-hundredths of a pound sterling.
The 5p coin is often pronounced five pee.
The obverse of the 5p coin has featured the profile of Queen Elizabeth II since its introduction on 23 April 1968.
The 5p coin replaced the shilling in preparation for decimalisation in 1971.
A smaller version of the 5p coin was introduced in June 1990.
The older 5p coins were withdrawn on 31 December 1990.
Four different portraits of Queen Elizabeth II have been used on the 5p coin.
The latest 5p coin portrait, designed by Jody Clark, was introduced in 2015.
The second and current reverse of the 5p coin features a segment of the Royal Shield.
The second reverse of the 5p coin was introduced in 2008.
